docs.title: What it would take to turn France’s debt woes into a bond ‘doom loop’
docs.text:
Global 
 What it would take to turn France’s debt woes into a bond ‘doom loop’
 Reshma Kapadia , Barrons 3 min read 9 Oct 2026, 06:29 AM IST 
 Summary
 Protesters are pushing the French government to boost spending even as bond investors pressure it to slash spending. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu vowed the government would unveil its policy response at month-end to the growing protests for increased spending even as investors sell off French bonds.
 The result is the current bond rout in France could fester for a while. France’s public debt has grown to 120% of its gross domestic product, and bondholders are pressuring the government to cut spending rather than increase it.
 Investors, meanwhile, are looking for signs that the fiscal mess upending the French bond market could spark further turmoil in the euro zone.
 The protests leaves France in a difficult bind ahead of its spring presidential elections. They raise the prospect the French government offers “expensive concessions” even though rising bond yields make that a less viable economic course, write Macquarie strategists Thierry Wizman and Gareth Berry in a note to clients. The duo see a potential “doom loop” between the protesters and the rise in France’s sovereign bond yields.
 During the European financial crisis in 2010 to 2013, the European Union pressured Greece, Italy and Spain to slash spending. As yields on sovereign debt rose, it hurt the balance sheet of banks that held it. That sparked capital flight as investors and savers took their money to more stable parts of Europe like Germany and the Netherlands. This “fragmentation” of Europe, the strategists note, is what brought the European Central Bank in to stabilize the situation and save the euro with extreme measures such as bond purchases and joining with the Federal Reserve for currency swap lines to give banks liquidity.
 The Macquarie strategists say they didn’t see deposit flight from France through August 2026, but the duo is on watch for any sign people are pulling their deposits out. That would be the first indication the European Central Bank could directly intervene to support the French market with liquidity, they say.
 Matt Eagan, head of Loomis Sayle’s full discretion team and a bond manager, doesn’t think Europe is in a crisis situation yet. But he adds, the “yellow lights are flashing.” France isn’t as vulnerable as the peripheral countries like Greece were during the euro zone crisis, in part because it’s almost too big to fail, but its fiscal problem is pernicious, he tells
 Eagan is keeping tabs on liquidity, and on auctions for French government bonds. “France mentioned they are thinking of increasing issuance of shorter-maturity debt, which suggests they know that it might be more difficult to build a book of demand for longer-dated issues at a reasonable price,” Eagan says. It’s a tact many other developed economies, including the U.S. are pursuing of late.
 In the near-term, the European Central Bank could help other countries vulnerable to contagion. But he thinks it is too early for the European Central Bank to step in to help France directly.
 “I don’t think the rest of the euro members would step in directly to help France without concessions from those governing the country, which is uncertain at this point until elections are held,” Eagan says.
 In the interim, other areas could begin to show strain. Eagan is keeping tabs on French banks, which have held up reasonably well, but will likely feel the heat as the crisis unfolds.
 Gavekal analyst Cedric Gemehl doesn’t see a repeat of the euro crisis because he thinks Europe will provide a backstop. He thinks the turmoil in Italy in 2018 after electing a populist government could be a better parallel.
 That said, he is keeping tabs on whether the prevailing assumptions currently priced into French bonds hold up. At the moment, he says, prices spreads suggest France will hit its 2026 budget target, that there will be some sort of fiscal consolidation in next year’s budget and that next year’s presidential election doesn’t result in a significant weakening in France’s public finances.
 “If these assumptions hold, they could provide an anchor for French spreads around the current levels,” he writes in a note to clients. “But there is a large probability that one or more of these assumptions will prove wrong, which would lead to a further widening in French spreads.”

 A glimpse inside Gaza shows how Israel’s military footprint is expanding
 Anat Peled , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 9 Oct 2026, 06:27 AM IST 
 Summary
 Israel is fortifying bases along a dividing line with Hamas as its military entrenches in the enclave. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 GAZA CITY—From an elevated perch on the eastern edge of Gaza City, a military official standing near bulldozers described the extent of Israel’s entrenchment in the Palestinian enclave. He pointed out two of Israel’s more than 30 bases in the territory, a third of which have been built since a ceasefire with Hamas took effect last year.
 Israel says it is using the outposts to guard a new dividing line with Hamas-held territory as its military clears out tunnels on the Israeli-controlled side—a job it says is almost complete.
 In the process, Israel is removing essentially every structure its troops encounter, military officials said. During a recent visit, The Wall Street Journal didn’t see any buildings remaining on the Israeli side of the line.
 The fortified outposts, which overlook a vast sea of rubble, often sit on high ground within the Israeli side of the so-called Yellow Line, the boundary separating Israeli-controlled territory from the rest of Gaza, according to analysis of satellite imagery and the official.
 “The Yellow Line is where you see the buildings that stand,” the military official said in the sandy ruins of Shuja’iyya, a neighborhood that saw repeated rounds of fighting during the war.
 Israel doesn’t allow journalists to enter Gaza on their own, saying the environment isn’t safe. Tightly controlled military embeds are the only way for international reporters to access the enclave. The Journal went on such an embed in early October. Many news organizations have criticized Israel’s policy on access for international journalists to Gaza and are pressing for independent access.
 Israeli officials say the military outposts and flattened areas are meant to reinforce Israel’s defenses after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed and some 250 hostages taken to Gaza.
 During the attack, militants overran civilian communities and front-line bases near the border, including an outpost staffed by unarmed female observers and the Erez Crossing, where soldiers were killed. Officials say Israel decided it needed wider buffer zones and a stepped-up military presence to protect civilian communities and soldiers.
 WSJ’s Anat Peled travels inside the yellow line in Gaza, where Israel has built around 30 military bases. One year after the ceasefire, satellite images reveal new outposts and fortified zones rising in the enclave.
 Buildings can hide tunnel entrances or be used by militants, the military said. Soldiers took the Journal through a sprawling tunnel in the outskirts of Shuja’iyya that they said had been discovered eight months ago. Israel has destroyed nearly all the tunnels on its side of the Yellow Line, two other military officials said.
 “The Yellow Line is a new border line—serving as a forward defensive line for our communities and a line of operational activity,” Israel’s military chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said in December.
 The Israeli military has expanded its control of Gaza from 53% under the terms of the deal drawn up as part of President Trump’s peace plan last October to around 70% now as it steadily shifts the Yellow Line forward, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
 The 32 Israeli outposts in service in Gaza are visible on satellite imagery, according to analysis by Jake Godin, a senior researcher at Bellingcat, an investigative consortium. The fortifications follow the Yellow Line and range from roughly 1 to 3 miles inside Gaza’s border with Israel.
 The Israeli government’s mapping agency last month briefly released high-resolution, unblurred images on the internet of northern Gaza from 2025 that showed several Israeli military outposts. The images have since been blurred by the Israeli government.
 Godin said that the outposts take several months to build and follow a similar rectangular layout. Most are paved, likely to ease access for military vehicles.
 They are filled with temporary structures for soldiers to sleep, eat and work in and have communication towers nearby.
 Military officials and analysts said the outposts were mainly being used for routine security tasks and were tactical rather than permanent.
 “The way all these bases are being built is a kind of reflection for the sad fact that Israel actually has no strategy,” said Michael Milshtein, a former Israeli military intelligence officer. “You are not building such sites if you want to stay forever or if you have any other idea.”
 The Israeli prime minister’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment.
 Under the second phase of Trump’s plan, Israeli troops were meant to gradually pull back from their positions as Hamas disarmed and handed control to a civilian administration and an international security force. But a year after the deal’s announcement, all of those elements are still stalled.
 Hamas has said it is willing to disarm, but it disagrees with Israel on the terms, while the militant group continues to assert its authority in the enclave. A committee of Palestinian technocrats hasn’t so far entered Gaza, and the international stabilization force lacks troops and agreement on its mandate. Funding for Gaza’s reconstruction remains stuck.
 No progress is expected ahead of Israeli elections set for Oct . 27, people familiar with the matter said. Netanyahu’s party is in a tough fight. Likud’s hard-right coalition partners have strongly objected to the terms of the Gaza peace agreement. Netanyahu has said that Israel rejects its terms.

docs.title: Why privacy must survive the age of AI: Not just humans, even the economy needs it
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Why privacy must survive the age of AI: Not just humans, even the economy needs it
 Aresh Shirali 5 min read 8 Oct 2026, 04:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 It's a sigh of the times. In a world under Big Tech’s watch and a country agog with Tata Sons’ private status, privacy looks like a quantum cat: both dead and alive. Scant concern for it isn’t just unjust, it could have economic consequences. Here’s how. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Nobody really has privacy anymore. I thought I should find a way to test this hypothesis, but it ’s futile. After all, some ‘effective altruists’ of the tech world even want the real world’s bugs mapped—for their own good, of course. Imagine waking up with a clunky exoskeleton; it would be impossible to handle a gadget, let alone get online, but equally hard to fall off the grid. Never mind humans, technology has clearly evolved. 
 My own effort to stay a social-media recluse got crushed by the might of ‘network effects,’ my will to keep my face off the internet in the fond hope of free speech in old age wilted a decade ago, and my ploys to mask myself for chatbots were foiled by the power of artificial intelligence (AI). 
 It’s futile to resist. So here’s the question that gets thrown at me every now and then: why is privacy such a big deal? 
 For an individual, the answer is clear. Not only is it critical to life and liberty as a basic right, it liberates thought—and action, so long as nobody else is hurt; and with luck, that can yield new ideas and spell progress. 
 Does the same apply to a private company? In matters of strategy, innovation and trade secrets that set it apart, yes. Privacy is key. As for finance, it depends on who else bears risk, which is why widely owned firms must disclose a larger template of data than those that are not publicly listed. 
 In the case of Tata Sons, being privately held lets it allot funds for charity and wealth creation free of external pressure. The argument that India needs it to go public for overall financial stability rests on the premise that a bigger window to its affairs would keep Tata’s apex company from harming others if it happens to stumble. 
 Since folly is folly, any entity can. On a visit to the Levant in 1873, Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata (1839-1904) joked in his diary that the rugged roads he found may have been built “to prove by a toil of actual experience that the way to Hell is paved with good resolutions.” The founder of the Tata Group might as well have been talking about business.
 Take the story of Tata Finance Ltd (TFL), which remained a flicker on my radar after a failed attempt as a college kid at buying its shares via its public offer of early 1991 (an issue-price cap had made it a lottery with dismal odds). Its goals struck me as worthy. 
 Yet, about a decade later, a subsidiary of a TFL sub-unit called Inshaallah Investments was wrapped up in a scandal over dodgy off-market equity trades that looked like a device to shuffle losses around. The Group’s top brass was alarmed, an official probe ensued, and in 2005, TFL was folded into Tata Motors . 
 The episode showed how corporate complexity could obscure fishy deals. It also exposed as flaky the notion of publicly listed companies being more angelic. 
 With AI sleuths now on the prowl, perhaps nothing can escape detection anymore. Yet, it puzzles me how the economy’s interests would be better served by wide investor scrutiny of Tata Sons if it thwarts both its majority owner’s will and charity mission. 
 While solvency woes at its operating units could rattle non-Tata financial firms, at least in theory, is this risk acute enough to justify a statist end to its ownership privacy? 
 But then, privacy often seems like a doomed cause even at its most basic level. Although India’s law to protect our personal data is finally going into force, it’s yet to grant us a modicum of control over what online operators know about us. 
 In a way, it’s already too late. Not just Big Tech, other ‘tech bros’ have been watching. Today, profiles held in cyber memory are said to be so vivid in their details that we may no longer be able to tell real folks apart from AI-crafted clones. 
 Nor should we pretend there’s no valid reason to keep any payment confidential. Cash is used not just for shady deals, but also for worthy causes that may suffer if their funding can be traced. Think of slums where the digital trails of UPI transfers let menfolk cramp the agency of women. Sometimes, do-gooders need masks too, and this is just one reason why India’s e-rupee ought to mimic cash as closely as possible. 
 The refrain that privacy is valued only by people up to no good is, in effect, a denial of diversity. For optimal outcomes, market theory posits that diverse views and cues must blend freely into signals—like prices—to guide the allocation of resources. 
 In other words, the blended agency of many mutual strangers would do a better job of putting an economy’s money, minds and much else to productive work than a few state planners likely to think alike. Granted, for all its efficiency, the market can go wrong; it may fail to factor in climate risks, for instance. 
 Even so, it’s an economic formula that mostly works, and for a market economy to thrive, it must constantly be fed with an endless variety of analyses, insights, motives, etc—for which privacy must make space. The same applies to the market for ideas. 
 As for my personal privacy, what spooked me last was a chatbot’s response to a query on quantum AI that took care not to reveal any filial motive. “Your dad’s theorem,” it guessed to my alarm, had been of help. It had ensured that a quantum neural network could work with real probabilities to deliver valid outputs. Uh-oh. 
 The author is editor of Mint Views.

News Sebi weighs allowing mutual fund distributors to become investment advisers Srushti Vaidya , Apoorva Ajith 3 min read 9 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST Summary If implemented, the move will allow individual MFDs to hold dual licences, similar to those held by institutions and other non-individual entities. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now Mumbai: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) is weighing whether individual mutual fund distributors (MFDs) should also be allowed to hold a registered investment advisor (RIA) licence, as it reviews the regulatory framework governing distribution and investment advice, according to two people familiar with the matter. “The working group is discussing whether individual MFDs should also be allowed to hold an investment adviser (IA) licence," said one of the two people on condition of anonymity. It is one of several issues considered by the working group set up by the capital markets regulator earlier this year to streamline norms governing MFDs and RIAs. The group's recommendation would allow individual MFDs to hold dual licences, similar to those held by institutions and other non-individual entities, the person added. The group was first mentioned by Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey in March. The review comes against the backdrop of a longstanding overlap between mutual fund distribution and investment advice. MFDs, who sell mutual fund products to investors and earn commissions from fund houses, also provide incidental advice on other financial products. However, the scope of such advice has not been clearly defined. An RIA, on the other hand, provides investment advice to clients for a fee and is permitted to advise on financial products beyond mutual funds. The recommendation, if implemented, would more clearly codify the investment advice given by MFDs. The norms could also help individual MFDs expand their businesses into advisory services. India has 1,048 RIAs and more than 100,000 MFDs. Mint 's queries emailed to Sebi remained unanswered. Pros and cons Individual MFDs argue that selling mutual funds without giving an investor advice on their other portfolio is often not possible. The concern is particularly relevant when investors have multiple financial products. An equity MFD may advise on equity products, while an insurance MFD may advise on insurance products; however, the investor may still have to deal with different intermediaries for different portfolio needs. “If an equity MFD is only allowed to give advice on equity products, while an insurance MFD gives advice on insurance products. An investor needs one advisor or MFD who can recommend a product based on a thorough analysis of the portfolio, combined with advice on how to generate better overall returns," said the second of the two persons. While allowing individual MFDs to become investment advisors could address the overlap, it would also create challenges, including potential conflicts of interest, dual compliance requirements and higher costs. “An (R)IA and an MFD would effectively be wearing two different hats. As an (R)IA, they are expected to provide advice without a commission-driven incentive. As an MFD , for the advice they give, they earn commissions from the products they sell,” said a senior RIA on condition of anonymity. “This could create an incentive to recommend a product that generates a higher commission, even when another product or a direct-plan alternative may be more appropriate for the client. Over time, an individual having both the licences could blur the distinction between fiduciary advice and commission-based distribution,” the person added. Then comes the compliance costs. Kartik Sankaran, an MFD with platform Happyness Factory, which manages assets worth more than ₹ 7,000 crore, said, “If an individual MFD has to gain an RIA licence to give a comprehensive financial plan, it would only increase their costs and compliance. Small MFDs would now need to have a compliance officer, additional documents and record-keeping, which will only add costs.” To be sure, such compliance costs would only be levied on distributors that also choose to enter advisory. Another RIA, also on condition of anonymity, said that having a dual licence doesn't solve the underlying problem. “An individual may struggle to manage two businesses, two sets of compliance requirements and two different incentives without mistakes or conflicts,” the RIA added. Sebi executive director Manoj Kumar said the working group's recommendations have been submitted to Sebi, and final guidelines on the matter will be issued soon, Cafemutual reported on 4 October. She has an experience of over three years in journalism, and has previously worked at Moneycontrol. docs.title: What six years of inflation mean for the midterms
docs.text:
Global 
 What six years of inflation mean for the midterms
 Owen Tucker-Smith , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 8 Oct 2026, 06:42 AM IST 
 Summary
 Inflation is cooler than it was four years ago, but voters are still paying much higher prices. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Four years ago, in the run-up to the last midterm elections, prices were rising more than twice as quickly as they are now. President Trump has repeatedly reminded voters of the 2022 inflation rate, blaming high prices on his predecessor.
 But Americans, weary from six years of quickly rising prices that have eaten away at their paychecks, might blame Republicans anyway as they head to the polls next month.
 Inflation sits at about 3.4%, far lower than its recent peak in 2022, when it topped 9%. Yet that means prices are still rising, adding to the higher costs consumers have absorbed in previous years. All kinds of everyday goods are 30% more expensive than they were in 2020. The prices of new cars, child care, beef and paper towels have all soared.
 Economists say that consumers generally focus more on the cumulative effect of years of steadily rising prices than on individual monthly metrics, and that it takes years for consumers to adjust to new price baselines. That helps explain why voters might be aggravated and still surprised when they see, for example, a $5 price tag on a gallon of milk.
 Prices for some items, like eggs, butter and cheese, have fallen over the past year. But newer signs of pricing pressure have emerged: Gas prices have lurched higher in recent months. Mortgage rates that have pushed past 7% and record home prices have shattered the playbook for buying a new home.
 “Voters have become incredibly impatient and disconcerted” by inflation, said Stephen Weymouth, a professor at Georgetown University’s business school who has studied the impact of inflation on elections.
 Slowing wage growth
 Over the past six years, prices have, on average, risen faster than wages.
 A swath of the population simply didn’t receive wage hikes to match the pace of inflation, which has eroded Americans’ purchasing power and likely contributed to an overall souring mood. The trend has been pronounced recently: In both July and August, inflation outpaced average hourly wage growth.
 Many employers have given raises that match inflation. But those raises don’t necessarily lead to happier consumers.
 When they give raises, bosses tend to tell staff that “you’ve done a great job at work and I’m rewarding you,” said Neale Mahoney, an economics professor at Stanford University. “So when you go to the grocery store and you see the price increase eroding away those wage gains, you see it as something being done to you.”
 Age of inflation
 Overall prices, as measured by the consumer-price index, have risen almost 29% in the past six years. During the six years before that, prices crept up at a third of that pace.
 Since the pandemic, prices have leapt in all corners of the economy: coffee, cleaning products, streaming services, hardware. A Hulu no-ads subscription jumped from around $12 to more than $20 and a New York City subway fare hit $3. The USPS “forever stamp” cost 55 cents in 2020. It has risen 49% to 82 cents.
 Big-ticket items
 Inflation data usually doesn’t include some of the expenses people care about most. U.S. out-of-pocket spending on healthcare per capita rose roughly 47% between 2020 and 2026.
 The cost of borrowing money also keeps climbing. Prices of housing, daycare and preschool, car maintenance and pet services have all grown more over the past six years than average hourly wages.
 Meanwhile, Americans have found themselves saddled with ballooning debt, further blunting the impact of income growth. A recent report by Century Foundation, a progressive think tank, found that in recent years, more than half of workers’ raises have gone toward debt payments.
 Strong spending, sinking confidence
 American consumers are spending big, and household spending has grown faster over the past 12 months as of August than it did last year. The S&P 500 is up 14% this year and the unemployment rate is low.
 So consumers might have a pretty good view of the economy—if it weren’t for the stubborn inflation squeezing their disposable incomes.
 While economists keep a close eye on the year-over-year inflation rate, consumers often compare prices they see at the store to benchmarks stuck in their head from years ago.
 And many consumers, when recalling what they believe they paid for a product a year ago, think they paid less than they actually did, said Michael Weber, an economist at Purdue University. They also notice price increases much more than they notice price cuts, said Weber.
 This might help explain why consumer sentiment dropped last month, according to the University of Michigan’s survey; sentiment among Republicans has fallen 20% since the start of the year.
 Impact on the midterms
 Inflation often punishes incumbents. In 2022 and 2024, high prices were the Democrats’ Achilles’ heel.
 Now, a president who made inflation a centerpiece of his political comeback is being asked to answer for the fact that on average, it costs around $50,000 to buy a car and around $60 to fill its tank with gas.
 It is easy for voters to connect the dots between Trump’s policies and high prices, Weymouth said. Consumers watched the prices of goods like bananas rise after the onset of reciprocal tariffs, Mahoney noted, and fall only slightly after those tariffs were rescinded.
 In a recent Wall Street Journal poll, 60% of respondents said Trump’s policies had made the economy worse.
 A White House spokeswoman said that the president had cut the cost of prescription drugs and added more than a million private-sector jobs to the economy.
 “The Democrats and Joe Biden destroyed our economy and crushed American families, and

docs.title: In a world of drones and self-driving cars, can technology secure flights from rogue pilots?
docs.text:
Opinion 
 In a world of drones and self-driving cars, can technology secure flights from rogue pilots?
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 9 Oct 2026, 08:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 The recent FlyDubai cockpit scare may make fly-by-wire tech seem like an aviation security solution. But the hitch has been that remote aircraft control technology is not free of risk either. Here’s the lowdown on the dilemma as it stands today. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The cockpit clash aboard a FlyDubai flight late last month that nearly cost the crew and passengers their lives exposed a worrisome vulnerability in civil aviation. 
 Flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the aircraft plunged after its co-pilot attacked the captain, who, despite being injured, managed to unlock the heavily secured cockpit door, enabling passengers to storm in and subdue the attacker. The plane landed safely but highlighted a paradox in aviation security. 
 Reinforced cockpit doors, mandated globally after 9/11, were designed to keep hijackers out—and unable to grab flight controls. Ironically, the high-security door was the obstacle to a rescue in this case as the threat came from within the cockpit. 
 But the big question raised by the episode is this: In this era of drones and self-driving cars , why can’t we count on remote intervention if a pilot goes rogue? 
 Technology to give computers greater control exists. Fly-by-wire (FBW), in development since the 1930s, replaced mechanical links with electronic signals. In 1972, the US space agency Nasa modified an F-8 Crusader to fly with a fully digital FBW system. Modern FBW systems process pilot commands digitally through onboard tech. 
 In military aviation, fighters like the F-16 can prevent ground collisions with systems that override pilot inputs. India’s Tejas has automated stabilizers in case a pilot blacks out or suffers severe spatial disorientation. National Aerospace Laboratories under India’s Council of Scientific and Industrial Research is working on ‘command-by-wire’ flight control. 
 Civil aviation has also been giving computers greater authority. Airbus aircraft use digital flight-envelope protections that can reject commands that defy safety limits, while Boeing typically prefers more empowered pilots, with systems resisting risky inputs rather than imposing danger lines. 
 Neither approach, however, crosses the red line of letting software or a remote operator snatch away control. FBW stops short of that because a tech system powerful enough to neutralize a rogue pilot’s actions would also create risks of its own. A ground link or onboard algorithm that can fly the plane pilotless could also be hacked, compromised or triggered by a software failure. 
 Boeing’s 2006 ‘uninterruptible autopilot’ patent illustrates the dilemma. It envisages detecting a security breach, isolating pilots and turning control over to a certified pilot on the ground through an encrypted satellite link. Hack-proof or not, it has not been implemented. 
 Machine authority is advancing in various ways. MIT’s Air-Guardian uses eye-tracking to monitor where pilots are looking and spot divergences in human and machine attention. 
 Garmin’s Emergency Autoland goes further, taking complete control if a pilot is unable to operate; it is designed to pick an airport, contact air-traffic controllers and land the plane on its own. Certified by the US Federal Aviation Administration, it has been installed in over 2,000 aircraft so far. 
 Although regulators may be ready to let software take control when a pilot is incapacitated, a rogue pilot who is conscious and capable of flying poses an entirely different threat. 
 The Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was saved by a captain who fought back, passengers who helped and crew who restored control. But relying on human bravery is dicey. Flight safety may need better tech support. The judgement calls that confront us are when to let software overrule a human and who takes that decision.

docs.title: Trump’s tariffs put a spotlight on forced labour. It isn’t going away.
docs.text:
Global 
 Trump’s tariffs put a spotlight on forced labour. It isn’t going away.
 Richard Vanderford , The Wall Street Journal 4 min read 8 Oct 2026, 06:55 AM IST 
 Summary
 ​The president’s use of forced-labor concerns to resurrect his tariffs faces a Democratic-led legal challenge, but America’s trade partners are toughening up their own laws either way. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The Trump administration resurrected its global tariffs by shining a light on forced labor. The tariffs face a court challenge, but the spotlight isn’t going away.
 After the U.S. Supreme Court in February shot down President Trump’s global tariffs—which relied on emergency economic powers—the administration turned to a new theory to partially revive them, accusing America’s trade partners of failing to take action against forced labor.
 Critics of the novel theory, including Democratic attorneys general and governors in more than two dozen states, last week asked a New York-based federal court to invalidate the new tariffs. The Trump administration turned to forced labor as a pretext, they argued.
 The White House didn’t respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.
 Regardless of the administration’s motivations, after the U.S. unveiled its forced-labor tariffs, a number of U.S. trading partners began to beef up their own legal regimes. Increased global scrutiny on supply chains is likely to continue no matter what the U.S. Court of International Trade decides.
 “It’s a big issue,” said Luis Lozano, the former president of Toyota’s Mexico unit and who now serves as chief executive of Mexico City-based advisory Odysseus Business Intelligence.
 “There’s more eyes,” Lozano said. “And there’s certain words as a global company you don’t want combined with your brand. One is ‘forced labor.’”
 Firm line
 Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, under which the Trump administration has imposed its new round of tariffs, lets the president take action against countries it finds have engaged in unfair trade practices. Various administrations have regularly used it over trade disputes in a number of sectors, from beer to green technology.
 The Trump administration supercharged the use of this legal power by taking action in July against 60 economies that it said had failed to adequately address forced labor, putting competing U.S. workers on an unfair footing.
 The U.S. has for decades taken a much firmer line on forced labor than its peer countries, first banning imports tied to the practice in 1930.
 In 2022, a tough measure specifically targeting China came into force. The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act effectively bans the import of any goods that can be tied to Xinjiang over human-rights concerns. Beijing has denied allegations of forced labor and other abuses in the region.
 That law forced many businesses to investigate their supply chains. Automaker Volkswagen, for example, in 2024 had a shipment of vehicles kept out of the U.S. after finding a single part traced to Xinjiang. VW said at the time it diligently investigates possible human-rights issues in its supply chains.
 As of August, the U.S. had under the UFLPA investigated about 44,000 shipments and denied entry to nearly 27,000 of those, most of them electronics.
 Mixed records
 Many U.S. allies have had more mixed records on forced labor. The European Union is planning to enforce its forced-labor import ban by December 2027, nearly a century after the first U.S. law was passed.
 Canada agreed to bar imports of goods made with forced labor as part of a free-trade agreement from Trump’s first term. But as of Oct. 2, Canada had held up just 53 shipments for inspection over forced-labor concerns and blocked two, one of textiles and another of seafood, according to figures provided by the Canada Border Services Agency.
 Canada is one of the countries that have scrambled to bulk up their forced-labor enforcement amid the U.S. push. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government proposed a tougher forced-labor law in June, about a week after the USTR filed a preliminary report that criticized the forced-labor records of Canada and other U.S. trading partners.
 “Regardless of whether one is for or against the tariffs, everyone has to admit that the 301 investigations have ignited conversations about forced labor in supply chains all over the world,” said Laura Murphy, a forced-labor researcher who advised the Biden administration.
 “In some places where advocates have been arguing for new action for a decade, we are seeing sudden movement,” Murphy said.

 The administration’s focus on forced labor is a welcome one, said Samir Goswami, director of forced-labor programs at Hague-based Global Rights Compliance, which works with governments and international institutions to promote international law.
 “We just needed to see enforcement through any instrument,” Goswami said.
 Colombia, for example, in late September banned the import of goods with any forced-labor touchpoint. India did the same in July.
 The USTR in September said it had brought 50 countries together for training on imposing and enforcing forced-labor bans. Mexico and Argentina committed on the sidelines of a G-20 meeting last week to work to eliminate forced labor from global supply chains.
 Countries around the world are unlikely to reverse their new forced-labor-related policy moves regardless of what the U.S. court decides, said Richard Mojica, head of the customs-and-import-trade practice at the law firm Miller & Chevalier.
 “Countries that have gone through this are unlikely to wind down any of these laws,” said Mojica, who advises large international businesses.

Opinion 
 Gen Z protests: Education and jobs in a free and open society are the top priorities of this generation
 Sanjoy Chakravorty 5 min read 8 Oct 2026, 02:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 In India, this is the bulkiest age cohort with over 400 million people. A youth bulge needn’t always boost growth. Unless smart policy choices are made on education and development, a demographic dividend can turn into demographic dissidence. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Tens of thousands of Indians are on the streets again. Led by a bolt-from-the-blue insurgent movement of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), citizens are protesting the unprecedented culling of voter rolls through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) ‘process.’ 
 They are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, under whose leadership millions of voters were ruled ineligible to cast their ballots. In West Bengal, this amounted to about 12% of the electorate. 
 This movement comes merely weeks after a similar agitation by the CJP led to the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as India’s education minister. 
 Recent youth movements in India’s neighbourhood have had momentous consequences. In Bangladesh, a student movement led, after a military intervention, to the resignation and exile of its then prime minister Sheikh Hasina in 2024. In 2025, a youth movement in Nepal forced the resignation of the prime minister and the installation of a caretaker government. 
 Similar unrest and political pressure elsewhere have led not necessarily to government collapse, but major policy reversals in Kenya, Indonesia, the Philippines and Peru. 
 All these movements are generally labelled ‘Gen Z revolutions.’ The same Gen Z label is being attached to the CJP-led protests in India. 
 The name ‘Gen Z’ comes from the US, where the need to categorize and label is an imperative of social scientists. People born after World War II have been assigned to generational cohorts spanning 15 years. 
 Hence, we have Baby Boomers (born between 1950 and 1964), Gen X (born between 1965 and 1980), Millennials (born between 1981 and 1996), Gen Z (born between 1997 and 2012) and Gen Alpha (born in 2013 and later). The Gen Z population is between 14 and 29 years old. 
 Is there anything other than age that the global Gen Z shares? An expert consensus suggests that it’s their digital immersion in apps like TikTok, YouTube and Instagram to consume entertainment and information. Entertainment and information are usually culture-specific, but what’s common is the many hours they spend online, how they create online identities and organize (socially and politically) online. 
 They also supposedly share concerns about climate change, inequality, corruption and established political parties. Gen Z is said to be left-leaning. One is reminded of the quote (usually misattributed to Churchill): “If you’re not a liberal at 20, you have no heart; if you’re not a conservative by 40, you have no brain.” 
 Just as relevant may be the question of whether there are things that almost all 14-29 year olds share regardless of when they were born, be it 1905 or 2005. That list is quite long. This is the age they seek mates, have children (though that is changing with delayed marriage and parenthood), finish education, find work and move. 
 The single most important determinant of migration propensity is age, and this is the age group that changes location with the least hesitation. These features are part and parcel of a mentality that is less fearful and more risk-oriented than that of elders, that can do romantic things like falling recklessly in love with a person or an idea . 
 This combination of digital immersion, online politics and risk-orientation may indeed be global, but there are major differences in the size of Gen Z between the developed and developing world. 
 In India, Gen Z is the bulkiest cohort. It has about 407 million people, or about 27.6% of the population. Indonesia’s share is a little less, and Nigeria’s a little larger. Together with the Millennials, Gen Z makes up roughly half of India’s people (and well more than half the electorate). In contrast, Gen Z makes up about 20.9% of the US, 18.8% of China, 15.8% of Germany and only 14.5% of Japan. 
 Think of the ways in which this demographic difference plays out politically. In the US, two-thirds of voters under 30 are left-oriented; the shares are roughly reversed for voters over 50. Had the share of younger voters in the US been similar to India’s, the Democratic party would win a lot more. 
 In Germany, where the youth vote is even smaller than in the US, the extreme-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) made stunning electoral gains in two states in the last month. The party’s vision of a better future for the older German electorate looks very much like a past in which there was nobody who looked or behaved differently. 
 What does a better future look like for the Gen Z-heavy Indian electorate? The political messaging from the Centre asks them to look at a glorious untainted past, supposedly last achieved a millennium ago. 
 But Gen Z is grounded in a present in which education and jobs are understandably top priorities. A better future for them is one in which they have decent, well-paid work in a free and open society. 
 But the reality is that youth unemployment is routinely higher than it is in the overall population and young people are routinely shut out of decision-making institutions and processes by entrenched older political elites. “These are kids,” they hear, “what do they know about how things work?”

 Iran and Houthis try to regain upper hand in Hormuz with spate of new attacks
 David S. Cloud , Summer Said , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 9 Oct 2026, 06:54 AM IST 
 Summary
 Crude prices rose sharply as Tehran targeted shipping traffic and Yemeni militants rained missiles on Riyadh. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DUBAI—Just last week, Iran appeared to have its back against the wall in its war with the U.S., its ports blockaded and its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz slipping. Now, Tehran is trying to regain the upper hand.
 Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen delivered a one-two punch against Persian Gulf oil producers in separate attacks on Wednesday night and Thursday morning that sent oil prices sharply higher and further shattered the sense of security in Saudi Arabia’s capital city.
 An oil and chemical tanker near Qatar was struck by several projectiles late Wednesday, causing casualties, according to maritime intelligence firm Vanguard and the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations agency. No one claimed responsibility for the attack, but officials in the region said Iran was likely behind it.
 The ship attack was followed by Houthi strikes Thursday in Riyadh, damaging aircraft at the international airport and forcing residents to take cover in the third straight day of attacks on the city.
 By increasing attacks on shipping, Tehran is seeking to break the stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz and increase pressure on Washington to reach a diplomatic settlement, analysts say. The limited military moves could raise oil prices and pressure President Trump before the midterm elections, while stopping short of another full-scale military confrontation that even Tehran doubts it can win.
 U.S. officials believe deferring a decision about whether to resume military operations against Iran will increase pressure on Tehran to make major concessions, including on its nuclear program.
 “Iran is clearly raising the pressure, while Washington is hardening both its rhetoric and military posture, but neither side has yet abandoned diplomacy,” said Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London. “This is precisely what makes the moment so dangerous. Both sides are trying to improve their bargaining position while sitting only one serious incident away from a much wider war.”
 The clashes underscored the region’s volatility and the difficulty that Trump faces keeping a lid on its conflicts at least until after midterm elections in the U.S. next month. Trump said Thursday that the U.S. won’t attack Iran before the election, citing “productive” talks with Tehran.
 “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections,” Trump said in a Truth Social post. He has also declined Saudi requests for direct U.S. military assistance against the Houthis, though the Pentagon is providing intelligence and other support.
 Oil prices rose, with Brent crude, the international benchmark, settling at $104.27 a barrel, up 4.1%, and WTI, the U.S. benchmark, up 4.1% to $91.87 a barrel. Surging energy prices weighed on stocks and treasury yields.
 Oil producers have increasingly relied on U.S.-protected tanker movements, ship-to-ship transfers outside Hormuz and pipelines that bypass the strait entirely. Saudi Arabia has also resumed exports from both its Gulf and Red Sea coasts after repairing part of the damage to its East-West pipeline following an attack last month.
 The Houthis are armed and trained by Tehran, but their escalating attacks against Saudi cities and oil facilities indicate that they are less cautious than their Iranian backers.
 The Houthis stepped up strikes inside the kingdom after Riyadh launched a campaign to retake Houthi-held territory in Yemen that threatened Saudi ship traffic through the Bab al-Mandeb, the heavily traveled gateway to the Red Sea. In response to the Saudi-led counteroffensive, long-range Houthi strikes have escalated into a daily occurrence in Riyadh, more than 500 miles north of the fighting in Yemen.
 Houthis said Thursday that Saudi aircraft had carried out several airstrikes across Houthi-controlled areas, including strikes targeting telecommunications networks in Yemen’s capital San’a, Hodeidah airport and Ibb, causing several casualties.
 “The fires targeting Saudi targets have not stopped, while warnings and strikes continue to escalate,” Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi said Thursday in a televised speech. “Saudi Arabia’s regime cannot achieve its objectives” of controlling Yemen, he added.
 At least two airplanes were struck in the latest attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Thursday. Falling debris from an intercepted ballistic missile hit a kindergarten and a medical-clinic complex, while workers in the city’s financial district, students at some international schools and diplomats were ordered to evacuate or take shelter.
 Residents across the city said they heard at least five huge booms Thursday morning but received no alerts or warnings on their phones from authorities. An empty commercial plane at Riyadh airport’s Terminal 4, which handles domestic flights, was hit in the afternoon and dozens of incoming flights were canceled or diverted.
 Foreign students at several international schools were shaken after spending part of the afternoon sheltering in place in windowless rooms, said a mother who spoke to parents at several of the schools.
 The Houthis’ military spokesman, Yahya Sare’e, said in separate statements that the airport had been hit by a ballistic missile and by two cruise missiles.
 The Saudi-led military coalition said it had shot down two ballistic missiles Thursday.
 It was at least the third time the airport had been targeted since Tuesday, when Houthi officials vowed to respond to airstrikes and missile attacks by the Saudi-led coalition agains

 Creators chase IP ownership. Legal bills follow
 Rudrani Chattopadhyay , Yash Tiwari 4 min read 8 Oct 2026, 01:05 PM IST 
 Summary
 Creators need ongoing advisory rather than occasional contract reviews, covering company setup, trademark filings, IP assignments, licensing and product agreements, and permissions for music, images and footage. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Creators are moving beyond brand deals to build their own intellectual property (IP), including shows, formats, products and businesses. But owning that IP also means incurring a growing set of costs, particularly legal and compliance expenses, which can run to ₹ 3-5 lakh a year.
 Building a creator-led business can involve company incorporation, trademark filings, IP assignments from editors and collaborators, licensing and production agreements, standards and practices (S&P) compliance, and marketing and advertising advice.
 Creators may also need licences and third-party permissions for music, images, footage, and other material used in their content, as well as advice on ownership and usage rights, and on emerging issues such as artificial intelligence (AI)-generated likenesses and personality rights.
 For Jaspal Singh Sindhal, a personal development and motivational creator who runs the YouTube channel Learn with Jaspal and has over 5 million subscribers, legal, compliance and IP work accounts for around 5-10% of his annual business and production spending, amounting to roughly ₹ 2-3 lakh a year. 
 “When you decide to build your own IP or launch products, you’re no longer just a creator. You’re essentially starting a business around your audience,” Sindhal said. Creators have to make the shift “from content creators to becoming solopreneurs or founders”, he added. 
 Sindhal’s estimate is broadly in line with the figure provided by Anupam Shukla, partner at law firm Pioneer Legal. Shukla estimates that creators can spend ₹ 3-5 lakh a year on building and protecting their IP, up from around ₹ 50,000-60,000 three to five years ago. 
 The cost varies significantly depending on the complexity of the business. Basic IP protection, such as trademark, copyright work and routine contracts, can cost around ₹ 1.5-3 lakh a year, Shukla said. 
 At the other end, creators building more complex IPs, such as direct-to-consumer ( D2C ) businesses or full-scale production studios, can spend ₹ 25-30 lakh annually on legal work, including equity structuring, licensing and merchandising agreements, cross-border trademark protection and monitoring for infringement. 
 For creators without agency or managerial backing, the economics can be harder to absorb. Legal and compliance costs are incurred while an IP is still being developed, creating an upfront expense at a stage when there may be little or no revenue to offset it, said Himadri Patel, a beauty and lifestyle creator with over 1.4 million YouTube subscribers and founder of fashion label Dri by Himadri.
 “A creator with an agency, manager or lawyer can get contracts reviewed and rights clarified without having to personally manage every detail. For someone working independently, the same process takes more time and often means paying for professional help from their own pocket,” she said. 
 Entry barrier
 The cost can also become a major bottleneck for creators building their first recurring series, said Sarah Sarosh, a beauty and lifestyle creator with over 1.5 million YouTube subscribers and founder of Impulse Coffees. 
 Unlike a one-off piece of content, a recurring series can involve writers, editors, production teams, guests, collaborators and brand partners, requiring creators to clarify ownership and rights across everyone involved. While brands typically have their own legal and commercial teams for collaborations, those responsibilities shift to creators when they begin developing their own IPs. 
 Legal and compliance costs are largely fixed and therefore weigh disproportionately on smaller and emerging creators, as they can consume a significant share of their early revenues, said Shukla. “Micro-influencers simply cannot afford specialized legal counsel,” he said, referring broadly to creators with around 10,000-100,000 followers. 
 As a result, some creators rely on generic online templates or AI-generated templates, or on standard-form brand agreements, which can give away IP rights or impose restrictive clauses. Saving on early trademark registrations can also leave their brand names vulnerable to infringement. 
 Sindhal and Patel, along with Alfiya Karim Khan, a modest fashion, beauty, and lifestyle creator with over 595,000 YouTube subscribers, estimated that legal, compliance, and related professional costs could account for around 5-10% of the budget for a creator-led project. 
 Khan estimates that making a digital series, from developing a pilot to producing its first batch of episodes, can cost ₹ 2-8 lakh. A larger YouTube production involving a crew, guests, travel or multiple locations can cost ₹ 8-30 lakh or more. Legal and compliance support alone can add around ₹ 50,000-2 lakh, she said. 
 Always on thin ice
 The most common legal issues these days include disputes over ownership and unauthorized use of third-party IP in creator-generated content, and use of names, logos, formats, characters and other IPs, as well as trademark disputes, said Kaushik Moitra, partner and practice lead for regulatory and IP-TMT (technology, media and telecommunications) at law firm Bharucha & Partners.
 Commercial disputes around payment, scope of deliverables, usage rights, and the continued use of content after a campaign or agreement ends are also common, he said.
 However, the costs can also vary depending on the nature of the content, said Moitra. A creator focused on financial advice, for instance, may need to meet additional qualification and disclosure re

docs.title: Rubio Says US Unapologetic About Power in Warning to Europe
docs.text:
In a speech on a hill in front of the Acropolis in Athens, the top US diplomat invoked Renaissance figures and Hellenic icons as he explained that the US was intent on revival and dominance. He also criticized other Western nations for letting their militaries wither and for ceding sovereignty to global institutions.
Rubio said the West finds itself “at a crossroads” with the next decade set to determine whether it “maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline.” 
“The United States has made its choice,” Rubio said. “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power — to take back control of our critical supply chains, to re-industrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.”
Rubio delivered his speech from the Pnyx in Athens, a hillside that served as the meeting place of the ancient Athenian democratic assembly and symbolizes the birthplace of direct democracy. His remarks — with rhetoric about the roots of democracy and the Acropolis in the background — had the occasional feel of an address by an aspiring head of state. 
President Donald Trump has frequently suggested either Rubio or Vice President JD Vance would be the best Republican candidate to succeed him in 2028, though Rubio has repeatedly said he has no plans to run and signaled support for a potential Vance campaign.
Rubio didn’t single out a particular nation in his speech. But his warnings to Europe — part of a four-day trip to Greece, Iceland and Portugal focused on defense and security with fellow NATO members — echoed past Trump administration critiques that have rankled European allies for their focus on cultural flashpoints, criticism of mass migration and the continent’s efforts to fight climate change. 
Relations between Europe and the US have deteriorated under Trump, who has repeatedly threatened Greenland — a territory of Denmark — and criticized Europe for not helping with his war against Iran. 
At the same time, European officials have pointed to the current stalemate between the US and Iran, elevated global energy prices and depleted US munitions stockpiles as a sign that US military power has limits. Trump’s recent decision to move US B-1B bombers from a UK airbase, citing terror threats, may also embolden Iran and Russia’s use of proxies to carry out sabotage attacks, according to current and former British officials. 
The Trump administration has spent the last two years trying to influence Europe’s political direction, pressing some of its closest allies to increase defense spending, loosen regulations and emphasize Christian values and history. 
“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lived here millennia ago,” Rubio said. 
Rubio has tended to take a more measured approach to Europe than others in the Trump administration, while some such as Vice President JD Vance have accused countries of shutting out far-right political parties. 
Rubio met with the Greek Foreign Minister Georgios Gerapetritis earlier Wednesday and extolled the virtues of the Mediterranean nation’s relationship with the US. He said the cooperation was valuable at a time of global uncertainty.

docs.text:
It noted that in the current situation, rate cuts are not a possibility in the near term. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra, in his speech, flagged the threat of inflation, citing that global inflation may increase sharply, prompting global monetary tightening. Thus, there could be further hikes or a pause on current interest rates. Notably, the RBI's decision does not mean banks will immediately or automatically increase fixed deposit rates. This is because while the repo rate influences deposit rates, banks also factor in liquidity, deposit mobilisation needs and credit demand before revising FD offerings. Overall, a higher repo rate could eventually lead to better interest rates on new deposits as banks work out their costs and try to lure investors. Thus, while the repo rate hike is for 25 bps, the transmission to FD rates may not be for the full 25 bps (or 0.25%), and market participants expect potential benefit only for new or renewed deposits. New investors or those looking to reinvest can keep a watch over the coming months for any official increase in interest rates of fresh FDs and recurring deposits (RDs) at public and private banks across the country. For existing investors, your rate of interest remains locked in for the remaining tenure / duration of your deposit. You can, however, choose to reinvest at a higher rate or take advantage of the FD laddering strategy to make the most of better rates in the future. docs.title: Turmoil ahead: Unhappy Europe is in the throes of a potentially major political shift
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Turmoil ahead: Unhappy Europe is in the throes of a potentially major political shift
 Rahul Jacob 5 min read 8 Oct 2026, 12:30 PM IST 
 Summary
 Protests in France have captured attention but youth restlessness is visible in Spain, Germany and other countries. Unlike the UK’s Andy Burnham, political leaders seem woefully out of touch. Sharp budget cuts are adding to discontent and making space for political extremes. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 More than 75 years after the end of World War II, conflict is spreading across Europe once again. But this time, the antagonism is within nations, and the contest, though fierce, is mostly non-violent and will be determined by the ballot box. 
 This week alone, Spain’s left-of-centre prime minister Pedro Sánchez dissolved parliament early and called for fresh elections after his plan to speed up housing projects in the country was blocked by his right-wing political opponents. 
 Sánchez was responding to nationwide outrage after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her Madrid apartment because she was unable to meet a rent increase, triggering mass protests over the country’s lack of housing. 
 In France, meanwhile, on Tuesday more than 250,000 people took to the streets to protest poor conditions in state schools, exacerbated by severe budget cuts of €43 billion intended to contain a widening deficit, placed at 5.4% of GDP. 
 Students were quickly joined by teachers and firefighters as the movement widened. The far-right front-runner for next year’s presidential election, Marine Le Pen, accused the far left of instigating violence. 
 Last week, the UK’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham told his Labour Party conference that he would, in effect, roll back Thatcherism. Burnham’s folksy manner and cost-of-living band aids have bolstered Labour’s prospects, which have also been helped by a spate of scandals affecting the anti-immigration UK Reform Party led by Nigel Farage. 
 Appointed prime minister this summer, Burnham moved quickly to lower taxes on energy for a fixed duration in response to the Strait of Hormuz conflict, giving people “breathing space” as fuel costs rose. He also boldly announced that his government planned to curb the rise in pension costs while finding funds for increasing the care of elderly people in need of attention at home. And he plans a survey of the UK to see if people want to undo Brexit. 
 The UK’s budget this month will offer an insight into how he plans to make good on his many promises. 
 It is too early to determine whether Burnham’s honeymoon will last, but the centre-left across the developed world could learn something from the man who was Manchester’s mayor for almost a decade. On top of that list should be Burnham’s focus on cost-of-living issues and his ability to signal a decisive turn away from technocratic neoliberalism. 
 By contrast, President Friedrich Merz of Germany, a corporate lawyer, who in breaks from politics was chair of the supervisory board of BlackRock Germany, and President Emmanuel Macron of France, a former investment banker, seem distant from ground-level concerns even as right-wing populists enjoy a huge upswing in their nations. Both these leaders have abysmal approval ratings in their respective countries. 
 Burnham’s upbeat style is somewhat similar to that of New York City’s mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose first year in office has been characterized by wild popularity as he tackles issues seemingly as simple as filling potholes, complete with TikTok videos to prove it, and more complex ones such as setting up low-cost grocery stores across the five boroughs of New York. 
 Regardless of who is in power, the real crisis in the West is a rise in short-term debt coinciding with rising interest rates. This is especially true of the US, UK and France. Inevitably, governments struggle to make the case that generous welfare spending on pensions and healthcare needs to be cut. If handled poorly, as in France, whose budget proposed to cut primary and secondary teacher positions against a backdrop of already overcrowded classrooms, mass protests could easily follow. 
 The problem is that Western governments spent too much in response to the financial crisis of 2008 and the pandemic, and now the cutbacks are falling inequitably upon public services even as stock markets have risen and housing becomes more expensive. 
 Spain has built fewer homes per capita than any high-income country in the past decade, according to the Financial Times . More than half of young adults live with their parents, compared with a third in 2005. The UK’s Labour government is well behind its targets for building new housing in the country. 
 In this environment of growing inequality and housing stress, budget cuts are an easy target for the far right or far left, in part because social media makes it easier for propagandists to make wild claims about an influx of immigrants, for instance, or the unfairness of cutbacks without those claims being evaluated by independent media. 
 Add to this general discontent the fact that a slowdown in job creation across the developed world—as in India—is disproportionately hurting new entrants to the workforce, and you have the makings of a series of political crises in the West. Youth unemployment in Italy is now at 20% Even in the US, a reliable job-creating machine, youth unemployment at 7% is twice that of older cohorts. 
 On Monday, I was awoken at 5.30am by the din of student protests outside the college of medicine in Paris. As the day progressed, the protests grew larger and louder still, with organizers saying the actual number across the country was half a million. 
 What’s remarkable was how unfazed my host and the city at large seemed. Perpetual political despondency in our world of inadequate governance and narrowing policy choices is now simply commonpla

Nifty 50 earnings seen rising 24.7% in Q2, best growth in 12 quarters
 Nifty 50 earnings seen rising 24.7% in Q2, best growth in 12 quarters
 premium 
 Nifty 50 companies are expected to post 24.7% year-on-year profit growth in Q2FY27, led by oil and gas, metals and automobile companies.
 Krishna Kant Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 7:15 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Brokerages and equity analysts expect high double-digit growth in the combined revenue and net profit of Nifty 50 companies during the September quarter (Q2FY27). The growth is likely to be driven by oil & gas and commodity producers, and automobile manufactures. 
 Among individual companies, the biggest revenue drivers are likely to be Reliance Industries Ltd (RIL), Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles and Hindalco Industries. The overall earnings growth is likely to be led by Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, Reliance Industries and Oil and Natural Gas Corporation — in that order. 
 According to various brokerage estimates, the combined net profit of Nifty 50 companies is expected to grow by 24.7 per cent on-year to ₹2.35 trillion, up from around ₹1.88 trillion a year ago but down marginally from a record high of ₹2.37 trillion in the first quarter of FY27. If achieved, it would be the best earnings growth on year-on-year (Y-o-Y) basis in 12 quarters. 
 The combined net sales (net interest income for banks and other lenders) is expected to grow by 17.4 per cent Y-o-Y to around ₹16.87 trillion in Q2FY27 from around ₹14.37 trillion in Q2FY26. At that pace, the topline growth would be the second best (after Q1’s 19.9 per cent Y-o-Y growth) in 15 quarters. 
 The revenue and earnings estimates for Q2FY27 and historical numbers for Nifty 50 companies include the figures for Wipro that was replaced in the index by BSE Ltd on September 30th. The Business Standard analysis does not include the earnings estimate or the historical number of BSE Ltd. The historical data includes the numbers of Housing Development & Finance Corporation that merged with HDFC Bank in July 2023 and Tata Motors Commercial Vehicle that demerged from Tata Motors (now Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles) in October last year. 
 The earnings estimates have been sourced from Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL), Kotak Institutional Equity, Nuvama Research and Antique Securities. 
 “We expect strong broad-based earnings growth, with aggregate earnings for the MOFSL universe surging 22 per cent Y-o-Y (the highest growth in 11 quarters) and ex-oil marketing companies (ex-OMCs) earnings to grow 24 per cent (the highest in 12 quarters). Earnings are likely to be anchored by financials, led by banks (private & PSU), NBFCs, metals, O&G (ex-OMC), and telecom,” write analysts at MOFSL. 
 Nearly 23 per cent of the incremental growth in the index companies’ combined net sales is likely to be accounted for by Reliance Industries which is likely to gain from a global rally in oil and petchem prices. RIL, Tata Motors PV and Hindalco Industries, are together likely to account for 41 per cent of the incremental growth in overall revenue in the second quarter on a Y-o-Y basis. In contrast, brokerages expect State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, Axis Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank to decline in revenue or net interest income due to faster growth in their interest expenses. 
 On the earnings side, Tata Motors PV is likely to be the single-biggest contributor to the Nifty 50 earnings growth in Q2FY27, accounting for nearly 15 per cent of the incremental growth on a Y-o-Y basis. It is expected to be followed by Reliance Industries and ONGC. Together these three companies will account for nearly 37 per cent of the index companies’ incremental earnings growth in the second quarter. 
 At the other end of the spectrum, brokerages expect ITC, Dr Reddy's Lab, Interglobe Aviation, Tata Steel and Cipla among others to report Y-o-Y decline in their net profit in Q2FY27. In all, the brokerages expect seven index companies to report a Y-o-Y decline in net profit in Q2FY27.

Agrichem majors face earnings cuts as weak demand, higher costs weigh
 Brokerages expect weak Q2FY27 earnings for agrichem firms as deficient rainfall, subdued demand and elevated input costs squeeze margins, prompting earnings downgrades
 premium 
 Revenue growth for listed majors in Q2 is expected to witness a decline of up to 12 per cent year-on-year due to the erratic monsoon and its subsequent impact on offtake and consumption of agricultural chemicals | File Photo
 Ram Prasad Sahu Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 09 2026 | 7:21 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Agricultural chemical (agrochem) companies are expected to report a weak second quarter (July-September/Q2) performance for 2026-27 (FY27), as erratic and deficient rainfall has hit demand. This, coupled with higher raw material prices and negative operating leverage, has crimped profitability. Brokerages believe earnings estimates for Q2 as well as FY27 are likely to be revised downwards to factor in the slowdown during the quarter and the near-term outlook. Given the multiple headwinds, the stock prices of top listed players, which are down 18-40 per cent over the past year, are unlikely to find support in the near term.
 Revenue growth for listed majors in Q2 is expected to decline by up to 12 per cent year-on-year (Y-o-Y) due to the erratic monsoon and its subsequent impact on offtake and consumption of agricultural chemicals.
 India’s monsoon ended 12.2 per cent below normal, the weakest since 2015, while El Niño is set to peak in November. While the kharif area is nearly flat Y-o-Y, dry spells in Maharashtra and Karnataka have put yields at risk.
 Nuvama Research expects the Q2FY27 show for its agrochem universe to remain weak, with Coromandel International expected to report a 56 per cent fall in earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation (Ebitda). The metric for PI Industries, Rallis India, and Sumitomo Chemical India is expected to decline by 36.7 per cent, 26.5 per cent, and 17.4 per cent, respectively. 
 Elara Securities expects its agrochem/fertiliser coverage universe to report a 7 per cent decline in revenues, while Ebitda and net profit are expected to drop by 13 per cent and 31 per cent, respectively. Analyst Prashant Biyani of the brokerage believes that an erratic monsoon left West and South India in a rain-deficit situation through most of August and September, hurting both fertiliser offtake and agrochem consumption.
 While agrochem consumption is weak due to lower pest and fungal infestation, the situation is not as dismal as in the case of fertilisers. This is due to limited placement in the first quarter (April-June/Q1), rains in the last 10 days of Q2 aiding consumption, and a lower base last year, the brokerage said.
 Dealers remain cautious about building inventory, as prices have trended downward since June after an initial spike in March-May due to the West Asia war. High-cost inventory may exert pressure on agrochem players in the near term. Brokerages expect the sector to face profitability pressures going ahead, given weak demand and higher input costs.
 Industry costs, according to Antique Stock Broking, rose during March-May, driven by higher technical (concentrated active chemical) prices, rupee depreciation, freight, packaging, and solvent prices.
 While some input costs have corrected to pre-war levels since June, analysts Manish Mahawar and Riju Dalui of the brokerage expect elevated freight and crude prices to keep overall input costs high.
 At the same time, weak demand and elevated channel inventory have limited agrochem companies’ ability to raise prices, which is likely to weigh on margins in the near term. Considering the challenging first half (H1) of FY27, the brokerage is trimming its earnings estimates and target prices for the coverage universe. Its key picks in the space are Sumitomo and Dhanuka Agritech.
 On the outlook, Elara Securities expects fertiliser raw material prices to peak and cool off gradually. On the demand side, recovery is expected from calendar year (CY) 2027 onwards as El Niño ends in February.
 Agri-input stocks should bottom out between October and December and rebound in H1CY27, followed by an earnings recovery from Q1 of 2027-28 onwards. Within the fertiliser space, it prefers Paradeep Phosphates and Coromandel, while within agrochemicals, it prefers Dhanuka and Bayer CropScience.
